posts.note: Privacy/HIPAA essay after Dobbs and the Change Healthcare breach. Main calls: DOJ will not meaningfully punish United Healthcare; HIPAA will be overturned via a Dobbs-based challenge. Wishes ('I would love to see a private right of action') and 'should fight' advice not logged.

Republished 2022 satirical 'evergreen press release' about the next mass shooting. Template predictions logged as sincere; the ironic closing line ('meaningful change is definitely going to happen') logged with sincere=false.
Review of existing weight-gain data (Blumenthal 2014, Petimar 2024). Closing 'Perhaps it's time to consider TMS as the First Line Treatment Option' is advice with no predictive reading; not logged.
Satirical Declaration of Independence rewrite celebrating the July 1 2024 CMS change allowing two TMS codes per day. 'Ought' demands about the medically unlikely edit are normative and not logged.
176-word podcast announcement (Deprescribe with Shawn Gill) with an Outro Health advisory disclosure; no forward-looking claims.
Celexa sexual-dysfunction review of the FDA label and Montejo 2001; all claims about existing data. 'Celexa I' implies a series but there is no explicit promise in the text.
Suicide-prediction essay co-written with David Carreon (DC sections). Analyses of the Papini 2024 Kaiser registry study, CDC trends and Haidt's thesis; no forward-looking calls found.
Announcement that the 8-part psychedelic primer series in the American Journal of Therapeutics is now open access. One conditional own-activity intent logged.
Launch of the Kindle book Inessential Pharmacology. Two own-product plans logged (print edition cover; other books in progress).
Reader question post ('five interventions on a desert island'); one conditional newsletter-programming promise logged.
Medical loss ratio essay (collab with an unnamed friend, presented in the author's voice). One structural claim with an implicit cost-growth prediction logged as borderline.
Podcast post on the proposed 2025 CMS Physician Fee Schedule with Grady Hannah (RAMHT). One newsletter-coverage promise logged; 'Let's push this one to number one' is a wish, not logged.
Satire mapping CMS 'medically unlikely edits' and the open comment period onto a birthday dinner. One timing claim about the CMS rule cycle logged; personal dinner jokes not logged.

statements.quote: It is going to create unbelievable amounts of pain and suffering for women and for the doctors who are attempting to care for them.
statements.context: Opening paragraph. 'It' is the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade (Justice Alito's opinion). The author expects the decision to cause large-scale suffering for women and for the doctors who care for them.
statements.note: Consequence claim about a court decision already issued in 2022; the predicted harm is ongoing and future.

statements.quote: The overturn of Roe might be the legal precedent to reclaim privacy, both for women, and for all of us.
statements.context: Thesis of the post: the author argues that the Dobbs reasoning (no federal right to privacy) creates an opportunity to challenge HIPAA and to rebuild privacy protections at the state level.
statements.note: Hedged; setup for the HIPAA-overturn call later in the post.

statements.quote: Now, in all practicality, there was almost no reason, previously, for anyone to engineer non-compliance solutions. Until now…
statements.context: After explaining that a practice that takes no insurance and processes no HIPAA transactions is not a HIPAA covered entity, the author implies that there is now a reason for practices and health-tech vendors to engineer deliberately non-HIPAA-covered solutions.
statements.note: Implicit and borderline: the forward-looking reading rests on 'Until now…'. Quote spans a paragraph break.

statements.quote: There will be no meaningful punishments brought to bear by the Department of Justice. It would bankrupt United Healthcare.
statements.context: On the Change Healthcare cyber attack (Change is a UnitedHealth Group subsidiary). The author predicts the federal government (DOJ) will not impose meaningful HIPAA penalties on United Healthcare for the breach, because a fine sized to the breach would bankrupt the company and the company donates heavily to politicians.
statements.note: Negative call on a federal enforcement outcome.

statements.quote: one of the ways United could get out of having to pay anything for those HIPAA fines? Just challenge HIPAA
statements.context: The author suggests United Healthcare could avoid HIPAA fines for the Change Healthcare breach by challenging the validity of HIPAA in court, using the Dobbs reasoning on privacy.
statements.note: Borderline: a possible strategy for United Healthcare rather than a prediction that it will take it.

statements.quote: If the challenge were based on the Dobbs decision? The Supreme Court will never do anything to undercut that
statements.context: Conditional: if United Healthcare (or anyone) challenged HIPAA on the basis of the Dobbs decision's reasoning, the author predicts the Supreme Court would not rule in a way that undercuts Dobbs, so the challenge would prevail.
statements.note: Conditional call about Supreme Court behavior.

statements.quote: I believe HIPAA will be overturned. The federal back door into our private information will close with it.
statements.context: Central call of the post: the author expects HIPAA to be overturned in the courts (via a Dobbs-based challenge), which would close the government's warrantless access to protected health information.
statements.note: Direct call with no date. Compound: overturn of HIPAA plus closing of the government 'back door'.

statements.quote: California’s laws already offer this, and other states could follow suit.
statements.context: 'This' is a private right of action for health-privacy violations. The author expects other states could follow California in enacting one, after the wish 'I would love to see a private right of action.'
statements.note: Hedged state-policy call.

statements.quote: Massive data breaches that leak our information are going to continue happening
statements.context: The author predicts continued large health-data breaches like the Change Healthcare attack; this is his reason for citizens to have a private right of action.
statements.note: Trend-continuation call.

statements.quote: I believe this will allow for all of us to robustly defend our protected and very personal health information from Hackers and government busybodies alike.
statements.context: 'This' is the combination of HIPAA being overturned and states enforcing privacy as an unenumerated right. The author expects the result to be stronger protection of health data against hackers and government access.
statements.note: Conditional on the HIPAA-overturn call.

statements.quote: United Healthcare defending its right to not pay a dime? It might be the one path to winning our right to privacy back.
statements.context: Closing line: the author expects a United Healthcare legal challenge to HIPAA (to avoid fines for the Change Healthcare breach) might be the path that restores a right to privacy.
statements.note: Hedged restatement of the HIPAA-overturn thesis.

statements.quote: A child psychiatrist reflects, in advance, about the next preventable mass shooting that will rock our nation to the core.
statements.context: Subheading that introduces the satirical pre-written press release. The author asserts that another preventable mass shooting will occur in the United States. The piece was first written July 18, 2022 and republished June 27, 2024.
statements.note: Satirical framing (evergreen press release), but the expectation of another mass shooting reads as sincere. Republished 2022 piece.

statements.quote: From what we know about the shooter at this time, he spent weeks/months planning the attack, and we do know he purchased the assault rifle/s legally, as well as the hollow point bullets that caused such horrible wounds.
statements.context: Template detail in the pre-written press release for the next mass shooting: the author predicts the shooter will have planned for weeks or months and will have bought the assault rifle(s) and ammunition legally despite prior disturbing statements.
statements.note: Pattern prediction inside satire; slash options are alternative fills. Written in press-release past tense about a future event.

statements.quote: A spokesperson for the NRA was reached, and offer the following statement: “This is America, and the NRA staunchly supports the reduction of gun violence through the addition of more guns into the hands of more good guys.
statements.context: Template in the pre-written press release: the author predicts the NRA's response to the next mass shooting will call for more guns in the hands of 'good guys' and blame mental illness rather than gun access.
statements.note: Predicted third-party reaction written as satire; own_claim true because the author forecasts the NRA's behavior.

statements.quote: This time, clearly, given the scope of the tragedy, it will be different, and meaningful change is definitely going to happen thanks to the actions of brave lawmakers representing this locality.
statements.context: Closing line of the satirical press release. Read literally it predicts meaningful gun-law change after the next mass shooting; the author's intended meaning is the opposite: no meaningful legislative change will follow.
statements.note: Ironic. The sincere reading is the inverse: the author expects no meaningful gun-law change after the next shooting.

statements.quote: These, in turn, may be acquired by UnitedHealth Group.
statements.context: Satirical Declaration of Independence rewrite aimed at 'the King of Big Health' (footnote guesses Andrew Witty). Joke that even the King's 'repeated injuries and usurpations' may be acquired by UnitedHealth Group, i.e., UHG keeps acquiring everything in healthcare.
statements.note: Joke; the literal claim is not a real expectation. Underlying sincere reading: UHG's acquisition spree continues.

statements.quote: disavow these usurpations, which, would inevitably interrupt our connections and fiscal viability of their industry—be it either pharma or med device!
statements.context: Parody of the Declaration's address to 'British brethren', here aimed at non-physician colleagues in pharma and medical devices: the author asserts that payer usurpations (coverage restrictions and hoops before reimbursement) would inevitably damage the fiscal viability of the pharma and device industries.
statements.note: Borderline: parody text with a conditional consequence; forward-looking only in a general sense.

statements.quote: If I am going to do that, it’s going to be published in a reputable journal.
statements.context: 'That' is a systematic review of all the data on a topic. The author states that any systematic review he does will be published in a peer-reviewed journal rather than in the newsletter; he then presents the 8-part psychedelic primer series in the American Journal of Therapeutics.
statements.note: Own-activity intent, conditional; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: So it's a little bit of a satire cover right now, but when I do the print for him, it should not suck so hard.
statements.context: Launch post for the author's Kindle book Inessential Pharmacology. He plans a print edition and expects its cover to be better than the current deliberately bad e-book cover.
statements.note: Own-product plan; 'should' is predictive here, not normative. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Are there other books I'm writing in the background? Yes.
statements.context: Book launch post; the author says he is writing other books, which implies further books will follow Inessential Pharmacology.
statements.note: Implicit forward-looking (more books to come); own activity. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I'm also asking this question to several colleagues, and it will become an article if you, dear readers, leave enough sassy comments.
statements.context: The author poses the 'five interventions on a desert island' question and says the answers from colleagues and readers will become a future newsletter article, conditional on enough comments.
statements.note: Own newsletter programming, conditional. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Big Health can increase profits only by increasing costs. The truth is costs have to go up or their profits go down, and they can't make their profits go down and keep their job.
statements.context: Medical loss ratio essay (collab with an unnamed friend). Because the Affordable Care Act caps insurer margin at about 20% of premiums, the author argues insurers can only grow profit by growing total health spending; implicit prediction that health costs will keep rising under the MLR rule.
statements.note: Structural mechanism claim; forward-looking only implicitly (costs will keep rising). Borderline.

statements.quote: More coverage of this open comment period is coming soon
statements.context: Podcast post: Grady Hannah (RAMHT co-founder) and two friends discuss the proposed 2025 CMS Physician Fee Schedule and its digital therapeutics provisions for behavioral health. The author promises more newsletter coverage of the open comment period.
statements.note: Own newsletter programming. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: The downside is these changes won't go into effect until 2025.
statements.context: Satirical piece mapping CMS 'medically unlikely edits' and the open comment period onto a birthday dinner ('Centers for Marriage and Snuggling'). The underlying real-world claim: any changes from the current CMS Physician Fee Schedule comment period will not take effect until 2025.
statements.note: Satire framing, but the timing claim reads as a sincere statement about the CMS rule cycle. Preceded by the wish 'We hope they will read these comments'.
